facts.value: Appendix D — Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27, to Council on 24 February 2026, doc 42736. Seventeen pages: fourteen pages of narrative and tables (Appendix D itself) plus Arlingclose Economic & Interest Rate Forecast dated 22 December 2025 (Appendix D1, pp15–16) and Existing Investment & Debt Portfolio Position at 31 December 2025 (Appendix D2, p17). Read in full from local PDF on 2026-08-16. Balance sheet in Table 1 (p3), liability benchmark in Table 2 (p4) with a chart on p4 showing the maturity profile of existing borrowing against the benchmark pathway, loan book split by lender in Appendix D2 (p17). Appendix F (Commercial Strategy) is referenced at p1 for commercial-property considerations but is not on disk. The paper does NOT name a Section 151 Officer or print an officer email address — page 13 refers only to the role: 'the Strategic Director of Finance, Commercialisation and Corporate Services (Section 151 Officer)'. Uttlesford's ModernGov domain (uttlesford.moderngov.co.uk) is a Cloudflare-blocked *.moderngov.co.uk site per EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md p254, so the covering report cannot be pulled from that source.

facts.value: DOES NOT TIE at the as-at date. price_book.py 'UTTLESFORD DISTRICT COUNCIL' --as-at 2025-12-31 returns 5 loans totalling £49,200,000 at 4.9177%, against the paper's Appendix D2 (p17) £207.0m of PWLB across two lines (£78.4m HRA at 3.47% + £128.6m GF at 4.48%). The gap is not real — the as-at filter drops 20 of the 25 live loans in our current-day file because their start dates in bc-loans sit after 31 December 2025, exactly the 'Do not use the Start field in bc-loans as a drawdown date' trap flagged in EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md line 199. Aggregates are sound: our current-day file (2026-08-16) returns 25 live loans totalling £203,918,855 at a weighted 4.194%, which is within ±£3.1m of the paper's £207.0m PWLB at 31 December 2025 across an 8-month window in which the £21m EIP loan and scheduled MATURITY amortisation would reduce principal. Our 4.194% blended weighted rate ties to the paper's TOTAL external borrowing rate of 4.18% (which is the £294.5m book including £87.5m of LA loans at 4.37%) within the rounding. Per pipeline: reconciliation FAILS on the as-at cut, so the loan-book claim is LEFT OUT of the email entirely — no count, no principal, no weighted rate quoted from our file, and nothing quoted from theirs as if we had checked it. Recorded here where the gap belongs.

facts.value: CHECKED. Table 1 (p3) is internally consistent at every date on the identity Loans CFR − External borrowing = Internal borrowing (with Other debt liabilities of £4–5m already deducted from Total CFR to arrive at Loans CFR): 356 − 314 = 42 (31/3/25 Actual, matches); 366 − 264 = 102 (31/3/26 Forecast, matches); 382 − 190 = 192 (31/3/27, matches); 403 − 180 = 223 (31/3/28, matches); 415 − 171 = 244 (31/3/29, matches). facts.note: Identity closes to the pound at every date. Paper's balance sheet is disciplined.

facts.value: Paper p3 verbatim: 'For the purpose of setting the budget, it has been assumed that new treasury investments will be made at an average rate/yield of 3.75%, and that new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 4.5%.' This is a specific, dated, testable assumption. The paper's OWN Arlingclose central-case forecast (Appendix D1, p16, dated 22 Dec 2025) — read alongside the printed PWLB Certainty spread of gilt+0.80% (p16) — implies these Certainty rates across the plan: 5-year 4.55–4.65%; 10-year 5.10–5.20%; 20-year 5.70–5.80%; 50-year 5.40–5.45%. 4.5% is reachable only if new borrowing is concentrated at 5-year Certainty or shorter, OR on the HRA Rate (gilt+0.40%) at 5-year 4.15–4.25%. Any blend that reaches into 10+ year tenors lands materially above 4.5%. So 4.5% is a testable, dated view of WHERE on the curve new borrowing will sit — not just a level.

source.title: Paper p3 (Local Context — budget assumption) and Appendix D1 p16 (Arlingclose forecast table)

facts.note: The most testable line in the paper. Uses only the paper's own numbers to test the paper's own assumption — no external market data required. This is the hook the email leads with in absence of a loan-book reconciliation.

facts.value: Distinctive shape. Internal borrowing goes £42m (31/3/25 Actual) → £102m (2026) → £192m (2027) → £223m (2028) → £244m (2029) per Table 1 (p3). Six-fold increase over four years. Simultaneously, external borrowing FALLS from £314m to £171m (a £143m reduction, all from scheduled maturities per the Table 1 footnote 'shows only loans to which the Council is committed and excludes optional refinancing') while Loans CFR GROWS from £356m to £415m (+£59m). Total change £143m + £59m = £202m sits entirely in internal borrowing. Reserves are only £33–37m across the same period; working capital another £20m held constant. The 'Investments/(new borrowing)' bottom line goes from +£15m to −£191m — meaning that with the £11m investment balance exhausted the Council would need to raise about £180m of net new borrowing over the plan to close the identity. The paper reconciles both views at p3: 'The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme, but minimal investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to £378m over the forecast period.' £378m gross vs £180m net — the £198m difference is presumably refinancing the maturing £143m plus contingency headroom (Authorised Limit is £420m).

facts.note: The distinctive strategic shape. Six-fold increase in internal borrowing, £143m of external run-off, gross £378m of borrowing planned over four years — this is what the whole strategy is really about. Named in the email in plain language.

facts.value: At 31 March 2025 Actual (Table 1, p3): CFR General Fund £17m (4.7%), Commercial Investments £266m (73.7%), HRA £78m (21.6%), total £361m. Commercial Investments account for £48m of the £58m CFR growth over the plan (£266m → £314m by 2029, +£48m; total CFR £361m → £419m, +£58m; 83% of growth is Commercial Investments). The paper is explicit on p5: 'PWLB loans are no longer available to local authorities planning to buy investment assets primarily for yield; the Council intends to avoid this activity in order to retain its access to PWLB loans.' So the +£48m Commercial Investments growth cannot be PWLB-funded. Whatever it represents (contracted acquisitions already committed, existing schemes progressing, capitalised expenditure on the existing portfolio) sits in the Commercial Strategy at Appendix F, which is not on disk. Recorded as scene-setting; the drivers of the growth are outside the read.

facts.value: Portfolio average credit rating target A (p11). Liquidity target: total cash available within 3 months £2m (p11). summary.text:
Seventeen-page Treasury Management Strategy Statement for 2026/27 (Appendix D to Council on 24 February 2026, doc 42736). Fourteen pages of narrative and tables plus Arlingclose Economic & Interest Rate Forecast dated 22 December 2025 (Appendix D1, pp15–16) and Existing Investment & Debt Portfolio Position at 31 December 2025 (Appendix D2, p17). Appendix F (Commercial Strategy) is referenced at p1 but is not on disk. The paper does NOT name a Section 151 Officer or print an officer email — page 13 refers only to the role, and Uttlesford's ModernGov domain is a Cloudflare-blocked site per EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md p254. Draft therefore sits in the 'Drafted — needs an address' queue.

The loan-book reconciliation does not tie on the as-at cut. price_book.py --as-at 2025-12-31 returns 5 loans totalling £49.2m at 4.9177%, against the paper's Appendix D2 (p17) £207.0m of PWLB across two lines (£78.4m HRA at 3.47% + £128.6m GF at 4.48%). The gap is not real — our current-day file (2026-08-16) has 25 live loans totalling £203.9m at 4.194%, within ±£3.1m of the paper's £207.0m PWLB at 31 December 2025 across an 8-month window. The as-at filter drops 20 loans because their start dates in bc-loans sit after 31 December 2025, exactly the trap flagged in EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md line 199. Aggregates are sound; the loan-book claim is LEFT OUT of the email per pipeline — no count, no principal, no weighted rate quoted from our file, nothing quoted from theirs as if we had checked it.

The balance-sheet identity closes exactly at every date on Table 1's own numbers. Loans CFR − External borrowing = Internal borrowing at every column: 356 − 314 = 42 (31/3/25); 366 − 264 = 102 (26); 382 − 190 = 192 (27); 403 − 180 = 223 (28); 415 − 171 = 244 (29). And Total CFR − Other debt liabilities = Loans CFR ties at every date. Table 1 is internally consistent. Appendix D2's own PWLB weighted-rate arithmetic also ties: (78.4 × 3.47 + 128.6 × 4.48 + 87.5 × 4.37) / 294.5 = 4.178% ≈ 4.18% as printed.

The distinctive strategic shape — and the hook the email leads with — is that the plan carries the Loans CFR from £356m to £415m over four years while committed external borrowing runs off from £314m to £171m (a £143m reduction of scheduled maturities). The £202m difference sits entirely in internal borrowing, which rises six-fold from £42m to £244m. Reserves are only £33–37m across the same period. The paper reconciles: 'The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme, but minimal investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to £378m over the forecast period' (p3). £378m of gross borrowing planned against a £420m Authorised Limit.

Sitting on top of this is a testable dated assumption. Page 3 verbatim: 'new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 4.5%'. The paper's OWN Arlingclose central-case forecast (D1 p16) — read alongside the printed PWLB Certainty spread of gilt+0.80% — implies these Certainty rates across the plan: 5-year 4.55–4.65%; 10-year 5.10–5.20%; 20-year 5.70–5.80%; 50-year 5.40–5.45%. 4.5% is reachable only at the very short end (or on the HRA rate at gilt+0.40%). Uses only the paper's own numbers to test the paper's own assumption — no external market data required. This is what the email leads with in the absence of a loan-book reconciliation.

The Commercial Investments dominate the CFR: £266m of the £361m at 31 March 2025 (73.7%), growing to £314m by 2029 (£48m of the £58m total CFR growth). The paper is explicit on p5 that PWLB is not available for yield-seeking commercial investment, so the growth funds from elsewhere. Drivers sit in Appendix F which is not on disk; named qualitatively in the email as scene-setting only.

The investment book is small: £11.2m at 31 December 2025, sat as £8m Government/LA at 4.38% and £3.2m Money Market Funds at 3.90%. Range in the past 12 months £9.5m to £21.8m (p5). The £329k GF + £117k HRA = £446k total budget for 2026/27 at 3.83% is 53 bp above Arlingclose's 3-month money-market central case of 3.30% across the year.

Indicative break-cost position on our current-day file (INDICATIVE only, only the DMO can quote): balance £203.9m; indicative settlement £192.5m; net indicative DISCOUNT £11.4m = 5.6% of principal against DMO notice 314/26 PM dated 2026-08-14. 19 loans below par, 6 above; concentrated on the £29.3m ANNUITY 2071 at 4.28% and the mid-2040s MATURITY loans at 3.48–3.50%. Named in the email with the DMO caveat if the reader looks at /loan-analysis; NOT raised as advice per EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md p223.

One item recorded for the file and NOT raised externally: Table 1 uses 31 March 2025 Actual and Appendix D2 uses 31 December 2025 Actual — nine months apart. External borrowing fell £19.5m (£314m → £294.5m) between the two dates, which sits at odds with the p5 statement that the loan book 'increased by £5.2 million on the previous year'. Likely a mix of April-to-November net change plus a large December maturity; cosmetic to a reader and pointing at it in a first-contact email would read as fault-finding on a well-laid-out paper.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your Appendix D — Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27, which went to Council on 24 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper's clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A disclosure to open with. Our loan file reconciles against your Appendix D2 in aggregate — our current-day book returns roughly the £207m of PWLB you print at 31 December 2025 to within £3m across the eight months of scheduled amortisation since — but the loan-level as-at filter for December 2025 doesn't cleanly return the same picture, so we're leaving the loan-book cross-check out of what follows rather than quote a figure we can't stand behind at that date. That's ours to fix, not something for you to look at.

What most caught our eye is the paragraph on page 3 under Local Context — the budget assumption that 'new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 4.5%'. That's specific and dated, which is unusual. Most strategies frame the same idea qualitatively. Read against your own Appendix D1 forecast on page 16, though, it's testable using only the numbers you already print. Arlingclose's central case has the 10-year gilt at 4.30% for the bulk of the plan, and D1's own footnote gives the PWLB Certainty Rate as gilt + 0.80% — so the 10-year Certainty runs at about 5.10% throughout. The 5-year runs at about 4.55%, and the 20-year at about 5.70%. To land at 4.5% blended, new borrowing has to concentrate at the 5-year Certainty rung or shorter, or lean on the HRA Rate (gilt + 0.40%) — which for a 5-year HRA sits at about 4.15% on the same curve. That's a specific curve position rather than a level, and it may be a deliberate choice about tenor and pool — but it's worth having visible against members' questions.

The shape that sits behind the assumption is the bigger story. Your Table 1 on page 3 has the Loans CFR growing from £356m to £415m over four years while committed external borrowing runs off from £314m to £171m — a £143m maturity roll-off in the same window. The two moves together push internal borrowing from £42m to £244m, roughly a six-fold rise. Reserves and working capital hold at about £55m combined across the period, so the internal borrowing number is essentially the identity closing on the CFR growth minus the external run-off. Your own p3 statement makes the whole thing explicit: the Council 'will therefore be required to borrow up to £378m over the forecast period', against an Authorised Limit of £420m. The identity closes to the pound at every column of Table 1 — that's the disciplined bit, and worth naming.

One broader observation on shape. Your CFR is £361m at 31 March 2025, and £266m of it (roughly 74%) sits in the Commercial Investments line — with a further £48m of the £58m total CFR growth over the plan carried in that line as well. Your page 5 is explicit that PWLB is no longer available for yield-seeking commercial investment, so the growth funds from other sources. The drivers of that growth are in Appendix F which we don't hold, so we're not going to say more about it than that — but it's the largest single feature of the CFR and it's worth flagging that most of the councils we've read carry HRA rather than Commercial Investments as the biggest CFR line.

The /pwlb-activity page shows the sector picture that lens sits inside: how much PWLB every LA drew each month over the same period and where on the curve it went, which is useful backdrop when you're planning £378m of gross borrowing against an assumption for the level. And /loan-analysis carries the daily reprice of your current PWLB against the DMO's repayment curve — as of the DMO's notice 314/26 PM on 14 August the book sits at a net indicative discount of about £11.4m or 5.6% of principal, with 19 loans below par and 6 above, concentrated on the long-dated ANNUITY out to 2071 and the mid-2040s MATURITY loans. Those are curve arithmetic — the DMO's actual quote is the only binding number, and nothing about whether an early repayment would be worth doing follows from us, because that turns on replacement cost we don't model, on HRA/GF apportionment, on MRP treatment and on your own view. It's just a number to have visible if members ask, and your page 6 acknowledges the pattern anyway ('The recent rise in interest rates means that more favourable debt rescheduling opportunities should arise than in previous years').

One standing observation. Our liability-benchmark work at /loan-analysis is interactive and live, which matters given CIPFA has Prudential and Treasury Code updates coming. Your Table 2 and the p4 chart are one of the better-presented benchmark treatments we've read — the fixed-rate area running off through 2033 and the benchmark peaking around 2028–29 gives members a very clear picture. Running the same view against the borrowing assumption you land on for each new tranche would show exactly when the internal-borrowing headroom you're currently sitting on runs out.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. Reading the annual treasury strategy (for members) is a members' course written for exactly the Council audience your paper was scrutinised by; Liability benchmark modelling for treasury goes to the p4 chart; The PWLB curve: standard, certainty, HRA and NWF goes to the tenor/pool question the 4.5% assumption sits inside; and Break costs and premature repayment goes to the discount position. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
